newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan savours Clinton win as sign of no U-turns.
newsitem.headline: Japan savours Clinton win as sign of no U-turns.

text.p: Japan, preoccupied with putting its own house in order, on Wednesday savoured President Bill Clinton's re-election as a sign there were no dramatic U-turns ahead in relations with its main ally.
Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto was unstinting in his praise for Clinton's victory, saying he congratulated the president "from the bottom of my heart".
"The people of the United States made a very great choice," Hashimoto told reporters.
And in an omen of likely calm waters in the years to the 21st century, Clinton and Hashimoto will celebrate re-elections within 24 hours of each other.

Hashimoto, head of the Liberal Democratic Party which will form a minority government after winning the most seats in a general election on October 20, goes through the formality of being re-elected prime minister by parliament on Thursday.
Top government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama told reporters Japan expected even closer and friendlier relations with the United States now that Clinton had been re-elected.
"We expect that our close and friendly relations will be reinforced. Unless we both make an effort to do so, it will not be good for us or the world," Kajiyama said.
"President Clinton's re-election reassures us of world peace and prosperity," Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda said.
U.S. ambassador Walter Mondale spoke equally warmly last week, telling reporters U.S.-Japan ties were "very solid".

Japanese officials and political analysts say that unlike past U.S. presidential elections, Japan is not worried about a zealous winner demanding immediate trade concessions, often a burr in bilateral ties.
"I don't expect the United States to get tough with Japan on economic issues," a high-ranking Japanese Foreign Ministry official told reporters.
"Trade issues (for the United States) now focus on China, whose trade balance may soon surpass Japan's," said John Neuffer, political analyst at Mitsui Marine Research Institute.
Neuffer said that during the campaign, Clinton had pretty much declared "I won the trade war" with Japan, so there was little worry of extra pressure on Japan to open its markets.
Seizaburo Sato, professor of international politics at Tokyo's prestigious Keio University, agreed that China, not Japan, was now in the hot seat with the United States on trade.
"Although there are still some (U.S.-Japan) bilateral trade issues in the fields of finance and aviation, they will not flare into serious friction," he said.
"It is not Japan but China which will have a far more serious trade conflict with the United States because of Bejing's growing trade surplus," Sato added.
For Tokyo, the southern Japanese island of Okinawa, home to the biggest contingent of U.S. military forces in Japan, remains the top political issue in bilateral ties.
However, at a summit in Tokyo last April, Hashimoto and Clinton set the stage for solving even this emotional issue.
A start was made at the summit in streamlining the size of the bases and further fine-tuning is scheduled to take place before the end of the year.
If there is one concern, it is that because ties are so strong at present, Japanese and U.S. officials may put them on the backburner, leaving the potential for crises to build up.

"U.S.-Japanese relations have entered into a period of drift, especially because of the lessening importance of security ties after the end of the Cold War," Shoichi Kuriyama, Japanese ambassador to the United States until last December, told a conference last month.
